query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Cr–Ni steels exposed to corrosive and irradiative conditions, a stable Cr-rich passivating oxide film—together with a radiation-tolerant microstructure—is chiefly responsible for their enhanced corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized Fe–Cr–Ni steels with controlled alloy composition (≥10 wt% Cr) and well-documented microstructures (grain size, phase distribution).
generation.intervention: Subject the steels to an in-situ synchrotron-based X-ray nanotomography experiment under a high-temperature, corrosive solution, while simultaneously exposing them to a controlled radiation flux. Periodically perform cross-sectional electron microscopy to explore oxide-layer development and microstructural changes.
generation.conditions: Simulated chemical-processing or nuclear-power reactor environment at elevated temperature (up to ~600 °C), pressurized water or corrosive media, and radiation levels reflecting typical service exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Dense, adherent Cr-rich passive oxide film coexisting with a fine-grained, radiation-tolerant Fe–Cr–Ni matrix.
generation.mechanism: Chromium preferentially oxidizes to form a compact protective film that resists dissolution and retards corrosion. In parallel, radiation-tolerant microstructural features (e.g., stable grain boundaries and second-phase nanoparticles) act as defect sinks to limit radiation damage and maintain oxide integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under these in-situ conditions, the steels featuring stable Cr-rich oxide layers and minimal microstructural disruption will demonstrate slower corrosion rates and less damage relative to steels with insufficient Cr or less radiation-tolerant microstructures.
generation.baseline: Matching low-Cr steels or steels tested under milder thermal and non-irradiative conditions, which are expected to develop less protective oxide layers and exhibit higher corrosion rates or oxide film breakdown.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to Fe–Cr–Ni steels with ~10–20 wt% Cr, typical temperatures ≤600 °C, and moderate radiation doses used in current nuclear/chemical facilities. Extreme doses or temperatures may lead to alternate mechanisms dominating.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of passivating oxide layers under prolonged or very high irradiation remains insufficiently characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare corrosion rates, oxide composition, and microstructure in a set of Fe–Cr–Ni steel samples with systematically varied Cr content under identical high-temperature, irradiative, corrosive exposure. Continuously monitor oxide-thickness evolution via in-situ synchrotron nanotomography while capturing microstructural changes by regularly extracting samples for cross-sectional electron microscopy and compositional analysis.
measurements: Oxide film thickness and uniformity over time
Elemental distribution of Cr, Fe, Ni, and other alloying elements in the oxide layer and grain boundaries
Corrosion current densities via electrochemical measurements
Radiation-induced defects and precipitation using TEM/EDX
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with significant Cr content exhibit neither improved oxide stability nor reduced corrosion rates relative to lower-Cr steels—or if they fail to form stable passivating layers under irradiation conditions—then the proposed mechanistic role of a Cr-rich oxide film for corrosion resistance is falsified.

The single-phase structure solves the key problem of poor corrosion resistance of ADSS alloy phase boundaries. The ATF cladding under normal working conditions is immersed in the PWR primary water for a long time, so the corrosion resistance of the cladding under this working condition will be an important guarantee for the safe operation of the reactor. Therefore, in this work, the corrosion behavior of these two HEAs under simulated PWR primary water was investigated. The corrosion products and corrosion mechanisms of these two HEAs are discussed in detail, and their corrosion resistance is evaluated.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC8200011) explored the corrosion performance of advanced high-entropy alloy coatings on carbon and stainless steels in a geothermal (high-temperature, corrosive) environment, emphasizing that manufacturing defects and coating composition impact corrosion resistance. Subsequent research (PMC9318428) examined specially designed stainless-steel-like high-entropy alloys in simulated pressurized water reactor (nuclear) conditions, finding that forming a dense and stable oxide scale (particularly in single-phase FCC formulations) enhanced resistance. Most recently (PMC9969177), reactive atomistic simulations in Fe–Ni–Cr alloys highlighted that dynamic oxide film formation and microstructural transformations (e.g., partial dislocation generation or BCC phase precipitation) strongly influence stress-corrosion cracking behavior. While passivating oxide layers, phase content, and defect control all show promise, it remains unclear how to specifically isolate and quantify the exact mechanisms governing robust and long-term corrosion resistance under combined corrosive and irradiative loads.
decision.unsolved: Despite significant progress in linking oxide films, alloy phases, and manufacturing effects to improved corrosion performance, it is not yet fully understood which factor most critically governs corrosion resistance under joint chemical and radiative service environments. The roles of radiation damage, evolving microstructure, and oxide film stability in sustaining corrosion resistance remain insufficiently characterized under the extreme temperatures, pressures, and chemistries found in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications. Methods to continuously monitor and decouple these influences in situ are still lacking.
decision.lever: Design an in-situ synchrotron-based X-ray nanotomography and cross-sectional electron microscopy experiment on Fe–Cr–Ni steels under simulated high-temperature, corrosive, and irradiative conditions. Systematically vary features such as radiation dose, solution chemistry, and temperature, and compare to an identical baseline steel exposed to non-irradiative or less aggressive environments. Monitor, in real time, the thickness, chemical composition, and adhesion of passivating oxide films alongside evolving local microstructure to determine how film formation and microstructural changes correlate with measured corrosion rates and stress-corrosion cracking behavior. Demonstrate that stable and adherent oxide layers and radiation-tolerant microstructures jointly reduce corrosion and mechanical degradation. Observe whether accelerated oxide breakdown or microstructural weakening occurs, which would falsify the protective-oxide-film hypothesis or identify other dominant mechanisms of corrosion resistance.
decision.why: Previous studies suggest that stable passive films, along with specific microstructural features, can confer enhanced corrosion resistance under harsh service conditions. However, data on how radiation damage and evolving microstructures interact with oxide films in real time are scarce. This experiment directly investigates those synergies under controlled, near-operational conditions, enabling a clear test of the hypothesized protective role of oxide films and the boundary conditions under which they break down for steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
